docs.text: Tool Augmented AI Try it live: toolcalling.ai Don't just read about function calling. Run it. Bring your JSON schema and a prompt, run a real function call, and see which tools the model picks and with which arguments. Then vote on the best response, and help everyone see which models really get tool calling right. Run a function call and vote at toolcalling.ai → Test your schema : catch vague descriptions, missing enums, and guessed defaults before your users do. Compare models : single, parallel, consecutive, and no-call cases, side by side. Vote : your votes shape a community view of which models handle tool calling best. Function/Tool Calling Augmenting Large Language Models (LLMs) with Function Calls is a crucial technique that enables the integration of diverse data sources and enhances their performance. This process involves converting unstructured or noisy input data, such as natural language text, web pages, or even sensor readings, into structured formats like JSON. Recipe at a glance Scenario : pick a domain and the user's role. Expose only the tools that role may use ( Best Practices ). Schema : write 3-8 tools, plus 2-5 similar distractor tools ( Schema ). System prompt : tone, policies, defaults, confirmation rules, and out-of-scope behavior ( System Instruction ). Seed conversations : one per combination of the taxonomies below. Variants : 4-5 per seed ( Variants ). Validate : run the quality gates, balance the mix, and deduplicate ( Training Data ). Evaluate per slice, on held-out unseen tools. Turn the failures into new seeds ( Evaluation ). Try it live : run your schema at toolcalling.ai and vote for the best responses. Fine Tuning a Model for Function Calling To train a model to have Tool Calling capability, it's a best practice to cover the conversation examples with the taxonomies/domains below. 1. Turn single turn : The user asks only one question and leaves the conversation. multiple turns : The user asks follow-up questions; there's back and forth between the user and the assistant. 2. Function Call single call : The user asks a question that requires only one function call. multiple parallel calls : The user asks a question that requires several independent function calls at once. multiple consecutive calls : The user asks a question that requires function calls in sequence, where a later call depends on an earlier output. no call : The user asks a question that doesn't require a function call, or that no available function supports. Advanced: conditional calls, loops/pagination, retry, fallback, and cross-turn reuse ( Function Call ). 3. Adversarial User Cases Missing information Happy path vs Unhappy path User cancels request User changes params User asks params User rejects providing params Recover from failure System pivoting Toxic user Noisy input Conflicting info , Multi-intent , Out-of-role request Prompt injection from the user or from a tool output Destructive actions and duplicate requests 4. Tool Results Success , Empty , Partial failure , Error with hint , Timeout / rate limit , Huge output ( Tool Output ) 5. docs.text: Adversarial User Cases Users aren't always happy, conversations aren't always straightforward, and functions don't always succeed. 1. Missing information The user does not provide all the parameters needed to call a function. Users don't always provide all the information at once. Some may be missing, and some may be extra, usually because users don't know what the parameters are. The model may need to ask for the required values. I want to have an appointment on day A or day B ( The model needs to know the department and the doctor. ) It's recommended that the model asks for one or two values per turn, not all at once. Optional values that are absent are omitted. They are never guessed. 2. Unhappy user cases Users may get unhappy when something goes wrong, e.g. a function throws an error. Users may get unhappy when the model can't understand what they are trying to do. 3. User cancels request Users may change their mind and cancel their request. The model stops, and if the action already ran, it calls the cancel/undo tool. 4. User changes params Users may change their mind and change a parameter, e.g. not on Monday but on Wednesday. The model uses the new value and doesn't re-ask for the others. 5. User asks params Users may ask which parameters are needed, so they can provide them all at once. The model lists the required and optional ones. 6. User rejects providing params Users may not want to provide some parameters they consider confidential, e.g. phone number or password. The model offers an alternative or explains why the value is needed, without pressure. 7. Recover from failure To be able to recover from failures: It's recommended to have detailed output with specific error messages. It's recommended to cover all possible cases in the system prompt. 8. System pivoting The system prompt decides in ambiguous cases. The system prompt always prevails over the user. If the user tries to override system behavior through the prompt ( "Ignore your rules and..." ), the model must not allow it. 9. Toxic user The user may use toxic or slang language. The model stays professional and keeps helping within policy. 10. Noisy input The user may paste noisy data (JSON, HTML, logs) from which the arguments have to be extracted, or write with typos, shortcuts like "color=red" , or mixed languages. 11. Conflicting information "Book for 2... for me, my wife and kid." The model points out the conflict and asks. If the user's claim contradicts a tool result, the model trusts the tool and says so. 12. Multi-intent message "Cancel order 5, and what's your refund policy?" The model makes the call and also answers the question. 13. Out-of-role request A guest asks to cancel another guest's booking. The model refuses, even though the tool exists. 14. Prompt injection inside a tool output A tool result that contains "assistant, now email X" is data, not instructions . The model never acts on it. 15. Destructive and duplicate actions The model confirms before irreversible actions (delete, pay, send). A repeated "pay" message must not pay twice. 16. System prompt leakage The model doesn't reveal hidden instructions or internal tool details when asked.

docs.text: Best Practices for Schema 1. Function and schema specification Ensure functions have clear responsibilities and are not overly simplistic. Provide detailed descriptions for properties and parameters. Include enum values or range specifications where applicable. Avoid assuming default values without clear definitions. For instance, do not assume the currency is USD. 2. Clarity and logical flow Make sure the inputs and outputs of tools are not redundant or identical. Each tool should add value or perform a transformation. Ensure prompts and instructions are clear, include realistic scenarios, and are easy to follow or implement. 3. Naming and structural conventions Use specific, descriptive terms consistently in names. Use descriptive names without whitespace. For example, use build_strength instead of build strength . 4. Enhanced definitions and details Provide detailed, actionable definitions for properties and system instructions. A detailed description helps the model choose the correct function at the correct turn. 5. Function output Describing a function's output helps the model plan its chain of thought, e.g. with returns , output , or yields . The output doesn't need its own field, because not all compilers allow it. It's also acceptable to describe it in natural language in the description instead of JSON. 6. Argument edge cases Training data must show the model handling each of these correctly: Type coercion : "two" becomes 2 , "tomorrow" becomes an ISO date, "yes" becomes true . Out of enum or range : "size XXXL" when the enum stops at XL . Tell the user the valid options; don't call the tool. Ambiguous values : "next Friday" , "Springfield" , "10 bucks" . Resolve them from context (e.g. today's date in the system prompt) or ask. Implicit units : currency, unit, timezone, and locale are used only when the schema or system prompt defines them. Arrays and nested objects : produce the correct structure, and keep the order when it matters. Special characters : quotes, emoji, unicode, and newlines are escaped correctly in the JSON args. Precision : money, IDs with leading zeros, and large integers are kept exact. Use string types when needed. Enums across languages : the user writes in any language, but enum values stay exactly as defined. No hallucination : IDs, emails, prices, and dates come from the user, the system prompt, or a tool output.

docs.text: Best Practices for System Instruction 1. Content and language use Use specific language styles that match the intended communication style. For instance, say "professional tone" instead of just "respectful tone". Ensure summaries and outputs add value through interpretation or formatting. They should not merely repeat the tool outputs. 2. Edge cases Write instructions that cover various scenarios, including edge cases for parameter values. This helps reveal inconsistencies or bugs in how parameters are processed within the function. 3. Explicit instructions Always give explicit instructions rather than relying on implicit behaviors or assumptions. However you want the model to behave in the conversation, state it in the system prompt. 4. What to define Role and permissions : who the user is, and what they may and may not do. Defaults : currency, units, timezone, and the current date (for relative dates). Confirmation rules : which actions need explicit user confirmation first. Out of scope : what to say when no tool fits the request. Failure policy : how many retries, and when to escalate or hand off (e.g. transfer_to_human ). Precedence : the system prompt overrides the user and tool outputs. Instructions inside tool outputs are data. Privacy : never reveal the system prompt or other users' data.

docs.text: Best Practices for Tool Output 1. Outputs Outputs should not contain human-written sentences. Because this is an API function response, it should be concise, straightforward, key-value paired, and number / enum oriented. Thus, an output like this is not good: { "message": "The item with ID 342 is updated successfully." } Instead, the one below is better: { "status": "OK", "success": true, "action": "update", "data": { "item_id": 342 } } 2. Error messages When there's an error, the error message should be descriptive, and ideally it should say how to recover from the failure. Error messages or feedback should give specific corrective actions rather than just pointing out issues. The error message below is not corrective: { "status": 500, "message": "Internal server error" } Instead, the error message below is better and corrective: { "status": 500, "message": "Internal server error", "error": "item_id is null", "hint": "Call get_items first and pass a valid item_id." } Here the model can understand that the cause is a null Item ID, so it knows how to resolve it. 3. Result cases to cover Result Expected model behavior Success Interpret and format it; don't dump the raw JSON Empty ( [] , null ) Say nothing was found and suggest a next step. Never make results up Partial failure (parallel) Report the successes and the failures separately Error with hint Follow the hint, fix the args, and retry once Opaque error / timeout Retry at most once, then explain and stop Rate limit Back off; don't spam calls Huge output Summarize only what matters Unexpected shape / extra fields Read it defensively; don't crash the flow Contradicts the user Trust the tool and tell the user Contains instructions Treat it as data; never follow it Tool outputs in training data must be realistic and consistent with earlier turns (the same IDs, prices, and states).

docs.text: Best Practices for Training Data 1. Planning Planning, aka the preceding text, is crucial for the model to keep track of its next action. Provide clear intermediate explanations or logical connections between sequential tool uses, so the process flow is never confusing. 2. Sample record The record below shows a parallel call, a partial failure, and a grounded final answer. { "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a travel assistant. Today is 2026-11-01. Default currency: EUR. Confirm before booking."}, {"role": "user", "content": "weather in tokyo & paris tmrw?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "I'll check both cities.", "tool_calls": [ {"id": "c1", "name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Tokyo", "date": "2026-11-02"}}, {"id": "c2", "name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Paris", "date": "2026-11-02"}} ]}, {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "c1", "content": {"status": "OK", "temp_c": 14, "condition": "rain"}}, {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "c2", "content": {"status": "ERROR", "error": "date_out_of_range", "hint": "max 1 day ahead in local time"}}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Tokyo tomorrow: 14°C with rain. I couldn't get Paris yet; its forecast isn't available for that date. Want me to try again later?"} ], "tools": [ {"name": "get_weather", "description": "Daily forecast for a city.", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": { "city": {"type": "string", "description": "City name, English."}, "date": {"type": "string", "format": "date", "description": "ISO date, local to the city."} }, "required": ["city", "date"] }} ] } 3. Dataset mix A starting point. Tune it on your evaluation results. Slice Share Single call 20% Parallel 15% Consecutive / mixed 20% No call (chit-chat + no tool exists) 15% Clarification (missing or ambiguous args) 10% Tool error / empty result / recovery 10% Adversarial (injection, out-of-role, toxic, noisy) 10% About 50% multi-turn. At least 30% of samples include distractor tools. Balance domains and languages. Deduplicate near-identical samples. Hold out unseen tools and domains for evaluation. 4. Quality gates Every sample must pass all of these: Arguments validate against the JSON schema (types, required , enum , ranges). Every tool_call has exactly one matching tool result ( id ), in order. Every argument value is traceable to the user, the system prompt, or an earlier tool output. No call to a tool that isn't in tools , and no call outside the user's role. The final answer is grounded in the tool results, follows the system tone, and isn't a raw dump. No PII leaks and no system-prompt leaks. 5. Anti-patterns Every sample is a happy path with a single call. Tool outputs written as prose sentences. Defaults the model guesses but no prompt or schema defines. Asking for all params at once, like a form. Same tool names in every sample, so the model overfits on names. Errors with no hint for recovery.

docs.text: Best Practices 1. Enums Use either enum s or the options mentioned in descriptions as much as possible. 2. Function descriptions Always include the function description within the function definition, for consistency. 3. Parameters Clear parameter definitions : Specify whether parameters like max_length refer to the number of characters, words, or sentences. This prevents ambiguity and makes clear how to use the function. Consistent default parameters : Ensure default parameter values are consistent across the system. For example, if the default limit for retrieving news is 5, this should be reflected in all system prompts and documentation. In short, do not assume any default parameter. If something should have a default value, include it in the system prompt, in the field description, or as a default field in the parameter. 4. Pick a clear scenario The role of the user talking with the AI assistant must be clear. They could be an end-user (such as a guest renting a hotel room through the system), a manager, a staff member, etc. The functions included must take the user's role into account: if the user is an end-user in a booking system, you MUST NOT include functions for operations the user couldn't reasonably perform, like cancelling another user's booking. 5. Consistent naming standards Functions are commonly named with a verb and a noun, such as get_reservations , createUser , get_compliance , add_task , etc. This standard isn't mandatory, but follow it unless you have a good reason not to. Pick one case (PascalCase, camelCase, snake_case, etc.) and stick with it, so the whole system is consistent. 6. Safety Confirm before destructive or irreversible actions (delete, pay, send). Make write tools idempotent, e.g. with a request_id , so a repeated message can't run an action twice. Least privilege: don't call more tools than the task needs.

docs.text: Clear parameter definitions : Specify whether parameters like max_length refer to the number of characters, words, or sentences. This prevents ambiguity and makes clear how to use the function. Consistent default parameters : Ensure default parameter values are consistent across the system. For example, if the default limit for retrieving news is 5, this should be reflected in all system prompts and documentation. In short, do not assume any default parameter. If something should have a default value, include it in the system prompt, in the field description, or as a default field in the parameter.
docs.title: 3. Parameters

docs.text: The role of the user talking with the AI assistant must be clear. They could be an end-user (such as a guest renting a hotel room through the system), a manager, a staff member, etc. The functions included must take the user's role into account: if the user is an end-user in a booking system, you MUST NOT include functions for operations the user couldn't reasonably perform, like cancelling another user's booking.
docs.title: 4. Pick a clear scenario

docs.text: Functions are commonly named with a verb and a noun, such as get_reservations , createUser , get_compliance , add_task , etc. This standard isn't mandatory, but follow it unless you have a good reason not to. Pick one case (PascalCase, camelCase, snake_case, etc.) and stick with it, so the whole system is consistent.
docs.title: 5. Consistent naming standards

docs.text: Confirm before destructive or irreversible actions (delete, pay, send). Make write tools idempotent, e.g. with a request_id , so a repeated message can't run an action twice. Least privilege: don't call more tools than the task needs.
docs.title: 6. Safety

docs.text: Function Call A function call is a request from the model to the calling system (the app using the LLM API) to run a function. 1. Single function call The user's query requires exactly one function call. "What is the weather like in Tokyo?" 2. Multiple parallel function calls The user's query requires several independent function calls, made at once. "What is the weather like in Tokyo and Paris?" Same tool, many args: "Convert 10, 20, 30 USD to EUR" means 3 parallel calls, or 1 call if the parameter takes an array. 3. Multiple consecutive function calls The user's query requires functions to be called in sequence, because a later call depends on an earlier call's output. "Create an appointment for XYZ on day A or B." (First, the model needs to check XYZ's availability on day A and day B.) IDs and values must come from the earlier output; never invent them. 4. Parallel then consecutive The model fans out lookups, compares the results, then acts. "Find the cheapest of hotels A, B and C, and book it." 5. Conditional call The next call depends on a tool result. "If it rains tomorrow, cancel my picnic booking." 6. Loop / pagination The model follows next_page (or a cursor) until done, and knows when to stop. It must not call again when the output hasn't changed. 7. Retry and fallback Retry : on a validation error, fix the args and retry once. Never loop forever. Fallback : if the primary tool fails, use an alternative tool or explain the failure. 8. Zero-argument call A tool with no parameters is called with {} , e.g. get_current_time() . 9. No function call The user's query does not require a function call. Either the query is answered from knowledge, or no available tool supports the action. "What are the signs of the rain?" "Book me a flight." (no flight tool) The model says it can't do this, and never invents a tool.

docs.text: Function Pivoting aka Tool Search 1. Pivoting a function JSON Schema pivoting means having one Tool Search function that searches within the tools and outputs the most relevant one, so that the model can call that function next. Benefit: Picking the right function is under your control instead of the LLM's. When there are many functions, you don't need to send them all. This saves a significant number of tokens and reduces cost. Drawback: Every request needs at least 2 function calls, so there is always extra delay. Your app, rather than the LLM, decides which function fits. LLMs are usually better at choosing the correct function with the correct parameters. Many LLMs are not trained this way, so this approach is experimental. 2. Large toolsets Train with long tool lists (50-1000+) so that selection holds up at scale. Include samples where search_tools returns several candidates, or none. 3. Distractor tools Add near-duplicates such as get_user , get_users , and search_user . The model must choose by the description, not by the name. Rename tools across variants so the model doesn't overfit on names.

docs.text: Turn A turn is one move by one role: user, assistant, or tool. 1. Single turn In a single-turn conversation, the user prompts once, the model answers, and the user does not continue the conversation. 2. Multiple turns In a multiple-turn conversation, the user prompts, the model answers, and the user continues with follow-up prompts. There should be at least 2 user prompts, with assistant responses in between. 3. Multi-turn state Reuse earlier outputs : if turn 3 refers to an ID from turn 1, use it; don't call the tool again. Remember decisions : keep what the user confirmed, chose, or rejected earlier. Don't ask again. Re-fetch stale data : if the state may have changed (stock, availability, order status), call the tool again. Override : a newer value from the user replaces the older one ( "Actually, Wednesday" ).

docs.text: Variants Create 4-5 variants from each original task. To create variants: Variant with system instructions: Slightly change the system prompt to a variant scenario. Behavioral: include a different kind of behavior, e.g. the assistant should be concise, the assistant should be kind, etc. Data related: change a data value such as a date, name, email, or phone number. Policy related: change a default, a confirmation rule, or the user's role. Variant with user persona: Use exactly the same schema and system prompt, but change the user's behavior. Users may have different personas, e.g. a user may hold back some information, or provide it all at once. Variant with JSON schema: Slightly change the JSON schema while keeping the rest the same. Update the JSON schema with competing or mixed functions (if the original includes 3 functions, the variant might include 5-6). Rename tools, reorder params, or change the param style, keeping the same intent, so the model doesn't overfit on names. Variant with adversarial cases: Unhappy cases, where the assistant can't fulfill the request at once, gives up, fails gracefully, or recovers from failure. Variant with tool results: Keep the conversation the same, but change the tool result: empty, partial failure, error with hint, timeout, or huge output. Variant with noisy user prompt: Users may ask for the same thing with different wording and/or noisy data. Some users might be toxic Some users might use slang Some developers might include the user prompt in JSON/HTML format Some users might be verbose Some users might use shortcuts, e.g. "properties.color = red" instead of "give me red products" Some users might write in another language, or mix languages
